cards.front: Why is a phylogenetic tree best understood as a hypothesis rather than a settled fact?
cards.back: A tree is a **hypothesis** about evolutionary relationships. Scientists revise it when new evidence changes which relationships are best supported.
cards.hint: Think about what happens when new evidence arrives.

cards.front: How do you work out which two groups on a tree are more closely related?
cards.back: Trace each lineage back to the **node** where the branches meet. Groups sharing a more recent common ancestor are more closely related. The order of tips alone does not show this.
cards.hint: Look at where the branches meet, not where the tips sit.

cards.front: Why do scientists look for shared derived characters when building a tree?
cards.back: A **shared derived character** is a trait that arose in a common ancestor and appears in its descendants. Groups sharing it are placed together on a branch.

cards.front: What is a node in a phylogenetic tree?
cards.back: A **node** is a branch point representing the most recent common ancestor of the lineages branching from it.
A **clade** is a common ancestor plus all of its descendants shown on the tree.
cards.hint: Think of everything that comes off one ancestral branch.

cards.back: A related group **outside** the groups being studied. It helps show which traits are ancestral and which are derived.
**Sister groups** are lineages that branch from the same immediate node.

cards.front: What does the root of a rooted tree represent?
cards.back: The **common ancestor** of all the groups shown on the tree.

cards.front: What steps do scientists follow to use DNA sequences to help build a tree?
cards.back: 1) Gather **homologous DNA sequences**. 2) Align them so corresponding positions line up. 3) Compare shared changes across many positions, often in several genes. 4) Use the patterns to evaluate possible trees.
cards.hint: Start with which sequences to compare.

cards.front: A student says the tip on the far left must be the most primitive species. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: **Position on the page** does not show how evolved a group is. Every living tip has its own evolutionary history, and rotating branches changes tip order without changing relationships.

cards.front: A student says a longer branch always means more time has passed. Why is this not always true?
cards.back: **Branch length** may represent elapsed time, the amount of evolutionary change, or nothing at all. Check the tree's scale or labels before deciding.

cards.front: A student says two living tips are drawn so one must have evolved from the other. What is the error?
cards.back: Both living tips descend from earlier **ancestors**. A tree with living tips does not show that one living group came from another living group.

cards.front: A student says that because two DNA sequences match at some positions, the groups must be closely related. Why is this not decisive?
cards.back: A match count is **not decisive** because a position can change more than once. Scientists look for patterns across many positions and genes.
cards.hint: What else could produce a matching position besides shared ancestry?
